Chapter 48

What I would do next, and what you now know

The project is complete and the suite is green, and it is still version one. An honest list of the next ten pieces of work, each with the chapter it would touch and the reason it was not done this week; a map from every Svelte and SvelteKit capability the course used to the chapter that used it; and how to keep the project current as the framework moves.

By the end of this chapter

Leave with a prioritised backlog you could start on tomorrow, a mental index of where each framework feature lives in the code, and a routine for upgrading without breaking the course.

A course that ends with “and now it is done” is lying to you. Software is finished when it is deleted; until then it has a backlog, and a good backlog is the most honest description of a project’s state. This one is ordered by what a real trip-planning team would ask for first, and every item names the chapter whose code it would change, because the chapters were written so that this list could be short.

The next ten

  1. A real tile server, behind a feature flag. The bundled world is the right default — offline, no keys, no third party — and it is too coarse for a city. A vector tile source is one origin in connect-src (chapter 46), one style swap in the map (chapter 29), and an environment variable in src/env.ts so the offline build stays the default. The flag is what keeps CI free of network.
  2. Invites by email. The invite *link* works; a mail with the link in it is a queue and a sender. The clean shape is an outbox table written in the same transaction as the invite (chapter 20) and a worker that drains it — the pattern the third project in this series built in full.
  3. Offline notes. Tiptap already holds the document (chapter 32); an IndexedDB copy and a queue of saveNote commands to replay on reconnect would make the notes tab survive a train tunnel. The read side is built: chapter 39 keeps every page a person opens and brings the live stream back when the network does. What is left is the write side, and the conflict policy it needs against a document somebody else may have changed in the meantime.
  4. Photos on stops. @sveltejs/enhanced-img handles the *static* images (chapter 23); uploads need object storage, a signed upload URL from a command, and a thumbnail pipeline. BODY_SIZE_LIMIT (chapter 47) is the first number to revisit.
  5. Rate limiting the public surface. Sign-in, sign-up, the join page and the route API are reachable by anyone. A token bucket keyed by IP in the security handler (chapter 46), backed by the database or memory, is a morning’s work and the first thing a penetration test would flag.
  6. A libSQL server instead of a file. The file is right for one machine; the moment there are two, DATABASE_URL becomes a libsql:// URL (chapter 14) and the rooms need a pub/sub that both processes share (chapter 19). Drizzle and the migration script do not change.
  7. Exporting the traces. The in-memory ring buffer (chapter 37) is for one process and a curious developer. Pointing the same provider at an OTLP collector is a different exporter in instrumentation.server.ts and nothing else — which was the point of putting OpenTelemetry in rather than a custom logger.
  8. More of the itinerary on the map. The map shows stops and the route; it could show days as colours, the selected stop’s neighbours, and a “fly to” on selection using the same interpolate() the globe uses (chapter 30).
  9. A fourth locale, right-to-left. Paraglide makes a new locale a new JSON file (chapter 21); an Arabic or Hebrew one would also exercise %paraglide.dir% and every inline-start in the CSS (chapter 23), which is why the tokens were written logically from the start.
  10. Accessibility audit with real assistive technology. The roles and names are there and the tests assert them; a session with a screen reader on the itinerary’s drag-and-drop and the date picker would find what tests cannot, and svelte-dnd-action’s keyboard mode deserves a chapter of its own.

Three things are deliberately *not* on the list. A native app: the web app is installable as it stands, and the map and the globe already work on a phone. A rewrite of the itinerary as a CRDT: the live query with last-write-wins per stop is the right trade for a few people planning a trip, and the fourth project in this series is the one to read if you need the other trade. And “more libraries”: chapter 40 spent as long on what was rejected as on what was chosen, and every item above is doable with what is installed.

Where everything lives

This is the index of the course by *capability* rather than by feature — the list to keep open when you start your own project and want to remember where a thing was done properly.

  • Runes — $state, $derived, $derived.by, $effect, $props, $props.id(), $state.raw, $state.snapshot, assignable $derived: chapters 07, 26, 27, 33. untrack and the effect-loop it prevents: ch. 26; untrack inside an attachment, so a snapshot does not rebuild an editor: ch. 32. Classes with runes in .svelte.ts: ch. 07, 26. (No $bindable: no component here offers two-way binding as its API, so none declares it.)
  • Templates — snippets and {@render}: ch. 22, 25, 27, 35; await in markup with {const … = $derived(await …)}, and a bare {const} where once is right: ch. 23, 25, 26, 30, 35, 37, 38 (there is no {#await} block anywhere; an await expression inside a boundary replaced it); <svelte:boundary> with pending and failed, read through boundaryMessage: ch. 27, 30, 35, 37, 38; {@attach} attachments: ch. 23, 31, 32, 42, and fromAction for a library’s action: ch. 27; class={[…]} and class={{…}} in place of the class: directive: ch. 25; keyed {#each} with a key that names the thing: ch. 30, 35, 38; animate:flip with svelte-dnd-action: ch. 27; {#key}: ch. 26, 33.
  • Reactivity utilities — MediaQuery, createSubscriber, scrollY from svelte/reactivity/window, SvelteMap versus a plain Map: ch. 43; Debounced from runed: ch. 37, 43.
  • Remote functions — query, query.batch, query.live, prerender, form, command: ch. 17, 18, 19; single-flight .updates() and requested().refreshAll(): ch. 18, 19, 33; invalid(issue.field()) and fields.x.as(…): ch. 18, 31; the transport hook: ch. 15.
  • Routing and loading — route groups: ch. 25; defineParams matchers: ch. 15, and the typed params a page takes through PageProps, with LayoutProps for a layout: ch. 25, 26; resolve() with typed route ids including groups, and paths.relative: false so the server writes paths too: ch. 25, 37; entries() with prerender and csr = false: ch. 36, 38; reroute for locales: ch. 21; +server.ts endpoints with CORS and OPTIONS: ch. 38, 46; the root layout with no load so prerendered pages do not bake a user in: ch. 25.
  • Hooks — sequence, handleFetch, handleError with kind on the server and in the browser, init, transport, reroute; hook types from @sveltejs/kit/hooks: ch. 15, 46, 47.
  • Configuration — everything in vite.config.ts: paths.origin and paths.relative, dynamicCompileOptions for a client-only custom element, tracing, csp in auto mode, csrf, version, preprocess for mdsvex, optimizeDeps for the browser tests: ch. 04, 44, 46.
  • Build and runtime — @sveltejs/package with publint and arethetypeswrong: ch. 09; @sveltejs/enhanced-img: ch. 23; read() for a bundled asset from an endpoint: ch. 17; a prerender function that is dynamic so a server render can fall back to it: ch. 17; customElement: true and customElements.define(…, Component.element), and a second Vite config for the element’s IIFE: ch. 38; $app/env’s browser, building, version: ch. 15, 26, 47; view transitions with onNavigate and an update banner from version.pollInterval: ch. 25.
  • The ecosystem — headless (Bits UI, TanStack Table): ch. 28, 31, 41; wrappers (svelte-maplibre, Threlte, LayerChart): ch. 29, 30, 31, 42; imperative through an attachment (Tiptap, GSAP): ch. 32, 23; compilers (Paraglide, mdsvex, Phosphor’s plugin): ch. 21, 36, 23; the survey and the rejections: ch. 40.
  • Proof — Vitest projects and vitest-browser-svelte: ch. 44; Playwright on the built server, in three projects — a desktop, a phone, and the phone at 360px — with two browser contexts on one trip and a test with JavaScript switched off: ch. 45; the container, the health check, the pipeline: ch. 47; the course’s own checks: ch. 47.

Keeping it current

The framework this course is built on moves every few weeks, and the versions in chapter 40 are dated for that reason. The routine above is the whole upgrade process, and the reason it is short is the reason the tests exist: verify is the same command in the pipeline and on a laptop, the suite runs against the built output, and the course reads the code rather than copying it — so a refactor that moves a function changes the course the next time it is built, and verify.js says which ranges need a human. When a SvelteKit release renames a thing, the Svelte documentation server and the svelte-autofixer used throughout this series are the fastest way to learn the new name; when it adds a thing, the question to ask is the one from chapter 01: is this the right shape, does it earn its bytes, could we remove it later.

You have built a collaborative application with a real-time document, three languages, a map, a globe, a shared ledger, an editor, a public API, an embeddable element, a published library, a container and a pipeline — and you have read every line of it with the reason beside the code. That is what “state of the art” means in practice: not the newest thing, but the right thing, chosen on purpose, and proven.

Checkpoint

  • You can pick one item from the backlog and name the files it would change before opening the editor.
  • You can find the chapter for any capability in the map above without searching.
  • You can run the upgrade routine end to end and say what each of its six commands protects.
